system.name: TrEnv
system.one_liner: a serverless platform that shares repurposable execution-environment sandboxes across functions and nodes using CXL/RDMA-based remote memory

content.subject: how a shared base rootfs (dev/sys/lib/bin) is reused across apps while each app's own overlay is mounted at /home/app

elements.role: root of the base filesystem tree, a reused mountpoint

elements.role: shared library/binary directories under the base overlay

elements.name: Base Overlay FS
elements.role: shared read-only overlay holding the common /lib, /bin file content, reused by every app

elements.name: Reuse
elements.role: brace calling out that /dev/null, /sys/, and Base Overlay FS are shared across apps, not duplicated

elements.name: /home/app/
elements.role: the one mountpoint that gets reconfigured per app

elements.name: App X Overlay FS
elements.role: App X's private overlay filesystem, holding its own home/app content

elements.name: App Y Overlay FS
elements.role: App Y's private overlay filesystem, holding its own home/app content

elements.name: On Host
elements.role: shows the actual host-side layer composition backing each app's /home/app view

elements.name: modification
elements.role: an app's private read/write change layer, unioned with the shared base to form its /home/app view

relations.what: root branches into the shared library/binary directories
the /dev/null mountpoint is backed by a character-device implementation
the /sys/ mountpoint is backed by sysfs
the shared directories are backed by files in the base overlay
App X's overlay is mounted at /home/app/ while X runs in this sandbox
App Y's overlay can instead be mounted at /home/app/, reconfiguring the same sandbox for Y
App X's logical /home/app view equals its private modification layer unioned with the shared /home/app base
App Y's logical /home/app view equals its own modification layer unioned with the same shared base

content.key_idea: TrEnv's sandboxes share one base rootfs (dev/sys/lib/bin) across every function, and reconfigure only the /home/app mountpoint to swap in whichever app's private overlay (base plus that app's own modification layer) is currently needed.
content.reading_order: left to right: the reused base tree (/, /dev/null, /sys/, Base Overlay FS) under the 'Reuse' brace, then the red /home/app/ mountpoint, then its two possible overlays (App X, App Y) and how each equals a base-plus-modification stack On Host

encoding.color_means: red marks a mountpoint (the caption's own legend); orange marks everything belonging to App X's overlay and its host-side layers; blue marks the equivalent for App Y; plain black/gray marks the shared, reused base filesystem

encoding.state_means: App X and App Y are told apart purely by colour (orange vs blue) and by which overlay box currently has a red arrow into /home/app/; both use the identical box+icon+stack template
encoding.marker_means: no numbered markers; the '=' and '+' signs on the right are the only symbolic notation, spelling out that a logical overlay equals a shared base layer plus a private modification layer
encoding.emphasis: the curly 'Reuse' brace under the left three elements, and the red mountpoint boxes singled out by the caption, are the two devices drawing attention to what TrEnv shares versus what it reconfigures
reusable_patterns: a shared/reused sub-tree set apart by a labelled brace, contrasted with a single reconfigurable mountpoint that different colour-coded overlays can be swapped into
an overlay-equals-base-plus-modification equation illustrated with a stacked-paper icon for each layer
weaknesses: no paragraph of body text discusses this figure directly, so the specific meaning of the 'char dev'/'sysfs' backing boxes and the stack order in 'On Host' are inferred from the image and general filesystem/overlay conventions, not confirmed by the paper's own words
App X's stack is drawn base-then-modification while App Y's is drawn modification-then-base, and it is unclear whether this ordering is meaningful or incidental

evidence: The red box indicates the mountpoint.
TrEnv introduces repurposable sandboxes, which can be shared across different functions

summary: Figure 9 illustrates an example rootfs reconfiguration in TrEnv's repurposable sandboxes. On the left, a base filesystem tree, rooted at /, is shared and reused (bracketed 'Reuse') across apps: /dev/null backed by a character device, /sys/ backed by sysfs, and /lib//bin/ backed by a common Base Overlay FS of generic files. The one mountpoint that changes per app is /home/app/ (all four mountpoints drawn in red, per the caption). Two red arrows show that either App X's Overlay FS or App Y's Overlay FS can be mounted there. On the host, each app's logical /home/app view equals its own private 'modification' layer combined with the shared /home/app base layer, drawn as small stacked-paper icons in that app's colour (orange for X, blue for Y). No paragraph of body text was found describing this specific figure, so several structural details are read from the image alone.

notes: No paragraph text mentioning this figure was found in the source paper (context file explicitly notes none); the description relies on the caption, the general abstract, and close reading of the image itself, so confidence is set to low. content.groups extended with a secondary 'comparison' group (prior listed only 'anatomy') because App X and App Y are drawn as two parallel instances of an identical overlay-plus-host-stack template; anatomy is kept as primary since most of the figure (the reused base tree) is not part of that comparison. content.base corrected from 'tree' to 'mixed' since only the left portion is a true parent-child tree; the right portion (overlay boxes, '=', stacked layers) is composition, not branching.
